title: Rolled oats: a yearly inspection fee for every mill, losses, exit and a higher long-run price
scenario: The market for rolled oats is perfectly competitive and is a constant-cost industry. It is in long-run equilibrium. The government then requires every mill to pay a yearly inspection fee, the same amount whatever the number of bags the mill produces. The mills and the numbers are invented, for practice.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Draw correctly labeled side-by-side graphs for the rolled oats market and a typical mill in long-run equilibrium. On the market graph, label the market price PM. On the mill's graph, show the mill's demand curve and label its profit-maximizing quantity qF.

rubric.point: Correctly labeled graphs: market with Price and Quantity, D and S; mill with Price (and cost) and Quantity, MC, ATC and AVC
accept: P and Q on both graphs
MC rising through the lowest point of ATC

rubric.point: A horizontal mill demand curve at the market price PM, labeled d = MR = AR = P (or MR = P)
accept: the market price carried across to the mill with a horizontal line

rubric.point: qF where MR = MC, at the lowest point of ATC
accept: the quantity where the price line meets MC, which is the minimum of ATC in long-run equilibrium

parts.sample: Market (left): Price on the vertical axis, Quantity on the horizontal, a downward D and an upward S crossing at PM and QM. Mill (right): Price and cost on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal; MC rises through the lowest points of AVC and ATC. A dashed line carries PM across to a horizontal line labeled d = MR = AR = P, which touches ATC at its lowest point. qF is where MR = MC, directly below that point, so P = ATC and the mill earns zero economic profit.

parts.label: B(i)
parts.prompt: Show the effect of the inspection fee on the mill's graph in part A by shifting the curve or curves that change.

rubric.point: ATC shifts up; MC (and AVC) do not move
accept: ATC2 drawn above ATC1, MC unchanged

parts.sample: The fee is the same whatever the mill produces, so it is a fixed cost: ATC shifts up to ATC2. MC and AVC do not move.

key.because: a yearly inspection fee, a fixed cost

slips.MC: The fee does not change with output, so it adds nothing to the cost of one more bag: MC stays put.
slips.S: In the short run the market supply curve is the sum of the mills' MC curves, which the fee does not move.

parts.label: B(ii)
parts.prompt: Explain why the fee does not change the mill's marginal cost.

rubric.point: The fee is a fixed cost, paid whatever the output, so it adds nothing to the cost of producing one more bag
accept: it is the same at every output, so the extra cost of one more bag is unchanged

parts.sample: Marginal cost is the added cost of one more bag. The fee is the same whether the mill makes many bags or none, so making one more bag adds nothing to it, and MC is unchanged.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Shade the mill's economic loss at the market price, after the fee.

rubric.point: The rectangle between the new ATC and the price at the mill's profit-maximizing quantity, from zero to that quantity, fully shaded
accept: (ATC2 - P) x q shown as a rectangle

parts.sample: The mill still produces where P = MR = MC, because MC has not moved. At that quantity the new ATC lies above the price, and the shaded loss rectangle runs from ATC2 down to the price, from zero out to that quantity.

slips.tc: That is total cost. The loss is only the part between ATC and the price.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: At the market price of $8 a bag, the mill sells 500 bags a day, and with the fee its average total cost at that output is $9. Calculate the mill's daily economic profit or loss. Show your work.

rubric.point: A loss of $500 (profit of -$500), with work shown: (8 - 9) x 500

parts.sample: Profit = (P - ATC) x q = <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>×</mo><mn>500</mn><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>500</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(8 - 9) \times 500 = -500</annotation></semantics></math> dollars a day, a loss of $500.

parts.label: E(i)
parts.prompt: Identify what happens to the number of mills in the rolled oats market in the long run, and explain why.

rubric.point: The number of mills decreases because mills are making economic losses
accept: mills exit because of economic losses

parts.sample: The number of mills decreases. Mills are making economic losses, so their owners can earn more by using their resources elsewhere, and some mills leave the market.

parts.label: E(ii)
parts.prompt: Explain what happens to the long-run market price of rolled oats compared with its level before the fee.

rubric.point: The price is higher in the long run: exit shifts market supply left until the price rises to the new, higher minimum of ATC, so mills again earn zero economic profit
accept: higher, equal to the new minimum ATC
exit raises the price until losses end

parts.sample: As mills leave, market supply shifts left and the price rises. It keeps rising until the remaining mills make zero economic profit, which now happens at the lowest point of the higher ATC curve. So the long-run price is higher than before the fee, and the market quantity is smaller.

parts.label: F
parts.prompt: Identify whether the price elasticity of supply of rolled oats is greater in the short run or in the long run, and explain.

rubric.point: Greater in the long run, because mills have time to enter or leave the market and to change the size of their plants
accept: long run: more time to adjust, including entry and exit

parts.sample: The price elasticity of supply is greater in the long run. In the short run each mill can change output only with the plant it has, but in the long run mills can be built or closed and plants changed, so quantity supplied responds more to a change in price.
